claims.text: Adding approximately 0.1–0.5 wt% yttrium to a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its resistance to high-temperature oxygen-induced degradation relative to the untreated alloy.
The yttrium addition will enable in-situ formation of a continuous Y2O3 surface scale.
The Y2O3 scale formed by the yttrium-added alloy will be adherent.
An untreated refractory high-entropy alloy based on elements such as Nb, Mo, W, and Ta rapidly oxidizes at high temperatures.
Yttrium preferentially oxidizes to form Y2O3 under the specified exposure conditions.
The Y2O3 scale acts as a protective barrier to oxidation.
The Y2O3 scale slows oxidation kinetics.
Improved scale adhesion and slower oxidation kinetics reduce scale spallation and substrate degradation.
In ambient air at 1100–1200 °C for approximately 100 hours, the yttrium-added alloy will have a significantly lower oxidation rate than the untreated alloy.
Under the specified conditions, the yttrium-added alloy will exhibit less oxide-scale spallation than the untreated alloy.
Under the specified conditions, the yttrium-added alloy will form thinner and more adherent oxide layers than the untreated alloy.
Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys suffer rapid oxidation and scale degradation because they form non-adherent oxide scales.
Prior evidence from Ni-based superalloys supports a beneficial role for reactive-element additions in oxidation resistance.
The quantitative effect of yttrium in refractory high-entropy alloys may differ from its effect in Ni-based superalloys because their alloy chemistry and oxidation behavior differ.
